prompt: [Sentence Completion] Because the new tariff made imported grain far costlier than the local harvest, city merchants who had long ignored nearby farmers began to ------- them, offering generous contracts months before the crops were even planted.
explanation: The tariff made local grain the merchants' best source, and 'offering generous contracts months before the crops were even planted' shows them actively seeking the farmers' favor - they woo them.
distractor_rationales: snub — 'offering generous contracts' is the opposite of rejecting the farmers
undercut — the merchants are seeking the farmers' grain, not underselling them; the tariff already made the local harvest the cheaper one
quarantine — nothing isolates the farmers; the merchants are drawing closer to them with contracts

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Far from securing the old dynasty, the emperor's decision to give each provincial governor a private army ------- the throne, for within a generation those governors answered to no one but themselves.
explanation: 'Far from securing' reverses the expected effect, and governors who 'answered to no one but themselves' show the throne's authority was being worn away from within - the decision subverted it.
distractor_rationales: repossessed — the decision gave power away to the governors; it did not take the throne back from anyone
safeguarded — 'far from securing' rules out protection
sanctified — making the throne holy is not the result of governors who 'answered to no one but themselves'

prompt: [Sentence Completion] The senators rushed the bill through in a single late-night session, hoping to ------- the governor's veto by passing it before he returned from abroad and could learn what it contained.
explanation: Passing the bill 'before he returned ... and could learn what it contained' is a way of getting around the veto - they hoped to sidestep it.
distractor_rationales: solicit — rushing so that he 'could learn' nothing shows they wanted no veto, not to ask for one
uphold — upholding his veto is the opposite of racing the bill past him
vindicate — nothing in their haste would prove his veto right

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Because the province had been promised self-rule and then denied it, its delegates were hardly the ------- partners the capital had hoped for; for a decade they stalled nearly every measure sent to them.
explanation: 'Hardly' denies the quality the capital wanted, and stalling every measure is what disproves it: the delegates were not easily led or managed - not tractable.
distractor_rationales: wizened — age is never at issue; stalling measures says nothing about how old the delegates were
solvent — finances are not mentioned; stalling measures has nothing to do with paying debts
voluble — stalling does not disprove talkativeness, so 'hardly' would have nothing in the sentence to deny

prompt: [Sentence Completion] So many coins had been clipped and shaved by dishonest traders that the currency itself became -------, and merchants began weighing every payment instead of trusting the value stamped on it.
explanation: Clipped coins caused merchants to stop 'trusting the value stamped on it' - the currency had become suspect.
distractor_rationales: vestigial — the currency is still in daily use; it has not shrunk to a leftover trace
usurious — excessive interest describes loans, and no lending is mentioned
sacrosanct — merchants no longer trusting the coins is the opposite of treating them as beyond question

prompt: [Sentence Completion] To ------- the rumor that the young king was a mere puppet of his uncle, his advisers had him sign every treaty in person before the assembled nobles.
explanation: Having the king sign every treaty himself in front of the nobles shows him acting on his own - the display was meant to rebut the puppet rumor.
distractor_rationales: validate — a public show of the king acting for himself works against the rumor, not for it
reiterate — repeating the rumor is not what a display of independence does
transcribe — signing treaties in person does nothing to write the rumor down

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Because every spring flood spread a fresh layer of silt across the delta, its farms stayed ------- for centuries, while fields on the unflooded plateau above wore out within a few generations.
explanation: Renewing silt keeps the land productive, and the contrast with fields that 'wore out' confirms the delta farms stayed green and flourishing - verdant.
distractor_rationales: saline — salty soil is a kind of wearing out, so it cannot be the contrast with fields that 'wore out'
terraced — the cut of the land is not the opposite of wearing out, and fresh silt does not shape steps
torrid — scorching heat is not what fresh silt from a flood produces

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Because the treaty's ------- were set far beyond anything the defeated nation could pay, its economy buckled under the debt, and the bitterness that followed helped spark the next war.
explanation: Payments imposed by a treaty on a 'defeated nation', large enough to become crushing 'debt', are reparations.
distractor_rationales: stipends — a stipend is a regular allowance paid to someone for service, not a debt that crushes the payer
sinecures — paid posts that need little work are not a sum a defeated nation is made to pay
truces — a truce halts fighting; it is not an amount that can be set beyond what a nation can pay

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Rather than abolish the ancient council outright and provoke its noble members, the new king chose to ------- it, quietly shifting its powers one by one to his own ministers until only its ceremonies remained.
explanation: Moving its powers elsewhere 'until only its ceremonies remained' keeps the council in existence but pushes it out of real affairs - he sidelined it.
distractor_rationales: repopulate — the sentence moves the council's powers, not its members
subpoena — no court or summons to testify is involved
rejuvenate — stripping its powers away is the opposite of restoring its vigor

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Although no law ever forbade the practice, the guild's ------- understanding that members would not undersell one another held for two centuries, enforced by nothing more than reputation.
explanation: No law stood behind it and only reputation enforced it, so the understanding was never set down in law or on paper - unwritten.
distractor_rationales: statutory — 'no law ever forbade the practice' rules out an understanding set down in law
rancorous — an agreement that held peacefully for two centuries was not bitter
quixotic — an impractical, idealistic scheme would not have held for two centuries

prompt: [Sentence Completion] To ------- the spring floods that had swept away the lower town three times in one century, the engineers cut a broad channel that carried the river's overflow harmlessly into the marshes.
explanation: A channel that carries overflow 'harmlessly' away is built to hold back the floods - to stem them.
distractor_rationales: swell — carrying the overflow away makes the floods smaller, not larger
simulate — the engineers built a real channel; they were not modelling floods
tabulate — cutting a channel is not counting or recording the floods

prompt: [Sentence Completion] After three failed harvests left nearly every farm owing more than it could ever repay, the town's moneylenders, rather than its lords, became its real -------.
explanation: When every farm is in their debt, the lenders hold the power the lords were supposed to hold; 'rather than its lords' points to rulers - sovereigns.
distractor_rationales: vassals — the indebted farmers are the dependents, not the lenders who are owed
squires — a squire is a knight's attendant; nothing in the debt makes the lenders servants
renegades — the lenders gain power through debts owed to them; they rebel against no one

prompt: [Sentence Completion] The framers deliberately divided the power to make war between the legislature and the executive, intending each branch to ------- the other's ambitions rather than to serve them.
explanation: Dividing power so that each branch works against the other's ambitions 'rather than to serve them' means each is meant to thwart the other.
distractor_rationales: underwrite — backing the other's ambitions is serving them, which 'rather than to serve them' rules out
transcend — dividing power does not lift one branch above the other's ambitions
satirize — a structural division of power is not mockery

prompt: [Sentence Completion] So thoroughly had the conquering empire ------- the local nobility, executing some and buying off the rest with titles and estates, that no revolt broke out for three generations.
explanation: Executing some nobles and buying off the rest brought them fully under control, which is why 'no revolt broke out' - the empire had subjugated them.
distractor_rationales: ransomed — the empire paid the nobles with titles and estates; it did not collect payment for them
radicalized — making the nobles extreme would cause revolt, not three generations without one
romanticized — idealizing the nobles does not fit executing them

prompt: [Sentence Completion] When the price of wool collapsed, the abbey responded with sweeping -------: it sold its outlying farms, dismissed half its laborers, and halted work on the new chapel.
explanation: The list after the colon - selling farms, dismissing laborers, halting building - is cutting back spending in response to lost income: retrenchment.
distractor_rationales: winsomeness — charm is not what selling farms and dismissing laborers shows
restitution — nothing is repaid to anyone who was wronged
virtuosity — dazzling skill is not the cost-cutting listed after the colon

prompt: [Sentence Completion] The builders aligned the temple so that sunlight reached its inner shrine on only two mornings a year, a design meant to ------- the pharaoh's claim to divine favor by making the gods seem to answer him on schedule.
explanation: Making the gods 'seem to answer him' gives the pharaoh's claim visible support - the design was meant to underpin it.
distractor_rationales: vitiate — a design that makes the gods seem to answer him strengthens his claim; it does not weaken it
sequester — the display was public; it did not hide the claim away
quantify — staging sunlight on the shrine does not measure the claim

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Because his decrees took four months to reach the distant provinces, the emperor's authority there was largely -------: governors received his orders with great ceremony and then did as they pleased.
explanation: Governors who honored his orders in form but 'did as they pleased' show authority that existed on paper but not in practice - theoretical.
distractor_rationales: tyrannical — harsh, absolute rule is the opposite of governors ignoring him
rapacious — nothing describes the emperor seizing wealth; the point is that his orders were ignored
retroactive — the delay makes orders arrive late, but the colon explains they were ignored, not applied to the past

prompt: [Sentence Completion] The general's victories made him so popular with the army that the senate, rather than reward him, began to regard him with ------- and quietly moved the legions nearest the capital out of his command.
explanation: 'Rather than reward him' turns away from praise, and moving the nearby legions out of his command is a defensive step taken out of fear - trepidation.
distractor_rationales: smugness — moving legions away from him is a defensive act, not self-satisfaction
veneration — 'rather than reward him' rules out deep respect
rapture — delight does not lead a senate to strip a general of nearby troops

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Because the coastal plain lay below the level of the highest tides, the settlers who drained it had to keep their dikes in constant repair; a single neglected breach could leave whole villages -------.
explanation: Land below the high-tide line, protected only by dikes, would be under water if a dike broke - the villages would be submerged.
distractor_rationales: thatched — roofing is not a consequence of a breach in a dike
razed — villages are razed by people tearing them down, not by water through a breach
quarried — a breach lets in the sea; it does not dig stone out of the villages

prompt: [Sentence Completion] To ------- the newly conquered provinces, the emperor settled veteran soldiers in colonies along every major road, where they could watch the local population and break up any gathering before it grew.
explanation: Soldiers placed to 'watch the local population and break up any gathering' are there to keep the conquered people under control - to subdue them.
distractor_rationales: vacate — he moved soldiers in; he did not leave the provinces
redeem — he already held the provinces by conquest; nothing is bought back
sanitize — breaking up gatherings is control, not cleaning

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Although the king's new coins held barely half the silver of the old ones, his treasurers insisted they be accepted at full value; predictably, merchants ------- the old coins, melting them down or hiding them away while paying their debts only in the new.
explanation: Since both coins were worth the same by decree, merchants kept the silver-rich old coins out of circulation - 'melting them down or hiding them away' - and paid only with the new: they withheld the old.
distractor_rationales: spent — 'paying their debts only in the new' rules out spending the old coins
struck — striking makes new coins; the old coins already existed and were melted or hidden
taxed — taxing is the state's act; the merchants are keeping the old coins, not levying anything on them

prompt: [Sentence Completion] The treaty made the river the border but said nothing about the islands in its channel, an omission that seemed ------- at the time yet proved costly: the two nations quarrelled over those islands for the next hundred years.
explanation: 'Seemed ... at the time yet proved costly' sets up a contrast with a century of quarrels, so the omission must have looked minor - trifling.
distractor_rationales: sinister — an omission that already looked threatening would not contrast with its proving costly
wanton — a deliberately reckless omission would not contrast with its proving costly
scandalous — an omission already seen as shocking would not contrast with its proving costly

prompt: [Sentence Completion] To ------- the farmers whose fields had been flooded to build the reservoir, the state granted each of them land of equal size in the valley below, along with three years' freedom from taxes.
explanation: Equal land plus freedom from taxes makes up for the fields the farmers lost - the state meant to recompense them.
distractor_rationales: surcharge — freeing the farmers from taxes is the opposite of charging them extra
repatriate — the farmers are moved to the valley below, not returned to a homeland
tithe — a tithe takes a tenth from someone; the state is giving to the farmers
